segments.text: [style: brisk, clear, architectural voice; steady studio cadence] Book Three, Proposition Twenty-Four. Similar segments of circles on equal segments are equal to one another. Let A E B and C F D be similar segments of circles standing on equal chords A B and C D. We are to prove that segment A E B equals segment C F D.

segments.text: [style: methodical, precise constructive cadence] Apply the segment A E B to C F D by placing point A on point C and the straight segment A B along C D. Because A B equals C D, point B also coincides with point D.

segments.style: speaking briskly, nimble, crisp, and composed
segments.text: [style: luminous, deductive geometric clarity] With base A B coinciding with base C D, if segment A E B does not coincide with C F D, it must either fall wholly within it, fall wholly outside it, or fall awry across it as C G D. It cannot fall wholly inside or outside, for by Three Twenty-Three two similar and unequal circle segments cannot stand on the same chord on the same side. Nor can it fall awry as C G D, for then two circles would intersect at more than two points—C, D, and their crossing point—which is impossible by Three Ten. Therefore segment A E B coincides everywhere with segment C F D, and by Common Notion Four, coinciding figures are equal; so segment A E B equals segment C F D, as was required to prove.

segments.text: [style: reflective, scholarly, architectural synthesis] Just as Book One, Proposition Eight follows from Proposition Seven by superposition, Proposition Twenty-Four follows immediately from Twenty-Three. Heath highlights Euclid's Greek verb parallassein—to fall awry—which separates two distinct impossibilities: nested arcs are ruled out by Three Twenty-Three, while crossing arcs as C G D are ruled out by Three Ten's two-point intersection limit.
